formation.title: The Sultanate Restored
formation.text:
Delhi stands once more as the seat of Muslim sovereignty over Hindustan. From the walls of Siri to the Qutb Minar, the city's skyline proclaims the power of the Sultan who has reunited these vast domains. The question now is what kind of sultanate this shall be. The martial traditions of Balban and the Khalji sultans beckon: an empire built on cavalry charges and the sharp edge of conquest. But so too does the vision of the Tughlaq administrators: a realm where Persian learning meets Indian wealth, where diverse peoples are governed through sophisticated bureaucracy rather than the sword alone. The Sultan must choose the path that will define this new era.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the cavalry thunder across the Gangetic plains!

modifiers.name: Sword of the Sultanate
modifiers.text: The Sultan commands the mightiest cavalry in all of Hindustan. Forged in the traditions of the Mamluk guard and the Khalji conquests, the armies of Delhi sweep across the plains with iron discipline and overwhelming force.

options.text: We shall build an empire of administration and culture.

modifiers.name: Throne of Hindustan
modifiers.text: From the seat of Delhi, the Sultan presides over a vast administration that bridges Persian refinement and Indian abundance. The court attracts scholars, poets, and merchants from across the Islamic world, and the diverse peoples of Hindustan find common purpose under enlightened governance.

advances.name: Mamluk Guard Tradition
advances.text: The institution of training enslaved youths as elite mounted warriors, inherited from the Abbasid and Ghurid traditions, produced the Sultanate's most fearsome cavalry.

advances.name: Iqta Land Grants
advances.text: The assignment of revenue-collecting rights over designated territories to military commanders in lieu of salary: the administrative foundation of the Sultanate.

event.title: The Iqta System
event.text: The iqta system, inherited from earlier Islamic states, has become the backbone of Sultanate administration. Iqtadars, military commanders granted revenue-collecting authority over designated lands, serve as both provincial governors and local military commanders. Under Sultan Iltutmish, these grants were made temporary and transferable, preventing the emergence of a landed hereditary aristocracy that might challenge the throne. The Sultan now faces a choice: tighten central control by demanding rigorous audits and frequent transfers, strengthening the crown but risking the loyalty of the military elite, or allow iqtas to become more stable, rewarding faithful service with security of tenure.

options.text: Centralize: the Sultan's writ must be absolute.

modifiers.name: Iqta Centralization
modifiers.text: The systematic audit and redistribution of iqta land grants strengthens the crown's direct control over provincial revenues and weakens the autonomy of local governors.

options.text: Let the iqtadars prosper in their domains.

advances.name: College of Hauz Khas
advances.text: In 1352 Firuz Shah raises a college beside the great tank of Hauz Khas at Delhi. Its masters are paid from the treasury, its students are lodged and fed, and those who finish go into the sultan's service as judges and secretaries. More are endowed on its model in the towns of the realm.

advances.name: Military Secretariat
advances.text: The Diwan-i-Arz maintained detailed rolls of every soldier in the Sultan's service, recording their appearance, their horses' brands, and their assigned equipment to prevent fraud.

advances.name: Khalji Market Controls
advances.text: The system of state-regulated markets and fixed prices instituted by Sultan Alauddin Khalji, enabling the maintenance of the largest standing army in medieval India.

event.title: The Sultan's Market Reforms
event.text: In the manner of Sultan Alauddin Khalji, the state has imposed sweeping price controls across the markets of Delhi. Three separate markets have been established: one for grain, one for cloth and manufactured goods, and one for horses, cattle, and slaves. Each is supervised by a shahna-i-mandi who reports directly to the intelligence service. Spies mingle among the merchants to ensure compliance. The purpose is clear: by fixing the price of grain at artificially low levels, soldiers can be paid modest salaries while still affording to feed their families. The result is a standing army of unprecedented size, historical accounts claim over 475,000 horsemen under Khalji's banner. Yet such controls breed resentment among merchants and farmers alike.

options.text: Enforce the controls: the army must be fed.

modifiers.name: Khalji Market Discipline
modifiers.text: The state enforces strict price controls on grain, cloth, and horses, enabling the maintenance of a massive standing army at manageable cost.

options.text: Loosen the markets: stability through prosperity.

advances.name: Tughlaq Fortifications
advances.text: The austere but massive rubble-masonry fortresses built during the Tughlaq dynasty, characterized by sloping walls, battered ramparts, and a focus on military function over decoration.

advances.name: Hasham Levy System
advances.text: The conscription of common infantry, the hasham, drawn from Hindu and Muslim peasants alike, trained and paid in cash rather than through land grants.

advances.name: Royal Karkhanas
advances.text: State-owned workshops producing arms, textiles, and luxury goods for the court and the army. Master craftsmen from across the Islamic world were recruited to work in these facilities.

advances.name: Barqandaz Tradition
advances.text: The mounted archers of the later Sultanate, skilled in rapid maneuver and harassing fire from horseback, drawing on Central Asian steppe warfare traditions.

advances.name: Sultanate Currency
advances.text: The standardization of coinage under the Delhi Sultans, culminating in Sher Shah Suri's silver rupiya: a coin so well-designed it became the basis of India's monetary system for centuries.

advances.name: Delhi Urbanization
advances.text: The transformation of Delhi into one of the world's great cities, with Ibn Battuta describing it in 1334 as the largest city in the entire Muslim world.

advances.name: Dagh-o-Chehra
advances.text: The military registration system of branding horses (dagh) and maintaining descriptive rolls of soldiers (chehra) to prevent payroll fraud and ensure martial readiness.

advances.name: Topchi Artillery Corps
advances.text: The adoption of gunpowder artillery by the Delhi Sultanate, drawing on Central Asian and Ottoman traditions. Topchi gunners served alongside traditional cavalry in the later Sultanate's armies.

advances.name: Suri Sarais
advances.text: The vast network of roadside rest houses built by Sher Shah Suri along the Grand Trunk Road, providing shelter, food, and security for travelers and merchants across the subcontinent.

event.title: The Imperial Sarais
event.text: In the tradition of Sher Shah Suri, the state has embarked on a massive program of infrastructure development along the great trunk roads of Hindustan. Every four miles, a sarai has been constructed: a walled compound providing shelter, food, and fresh horses to travelers. Each sarai contains a mosque, separate quarters for Hindu and Muslim travelers, a well, and stables. The total network exceeds 1,700 sarais, transforming what were once perilous journeys through bandit-infested countryside into routine commerce. Merchants report that goods can now travel from Sonargaon in Bengal to the Indus frontier in weeks rather than months.

modifiers.name: Suri Imperial Highway
modifiers.text: The expansion of the Grand Trunk Road and construction of sarais along its length has transformed overland commerce, connecting Bengal to the Indus in a continuous ribbon of trade.

options.text: The roads are built. Now let trade flow.

advances.name: Suri Administrative Reform
advances.text: The reorganization of provincial government under Sher Shah Suri, dividing the empire into sarkars and parganas with systematic revenue assessment and professional administration.

advances.name: Indo-Islamic Architecture
advances.text: The distinctive fusion of Persian and Indian architectural traditions, from the pointed arches and geometric calligraphy of the Khalji era to the double domes and Bangla roofing of the Lodis.

advances.name: Suri Military Reform
advances.text: Sher Shah Suri's reorganization of the army into a disciplined, centrally-paid force with standardized equipment, replacing the feudal levy system with professional infantry.

advances.name: Grand Trunk Expansion
advances.text: The continued development of Hindustan's road network, with shade trees, milestones, and bridges connecting the empire's far-flung provinces to the capital.

advances.name: Centralized Revenue
advances.text: The systematic measurement and assessment of agricultural land across the Sultanate, replacing estimate-based taxation with survey-based revenue extraction.

advances.name: Reformed Sultanate Army
advances.text: The modernization of Delhi's military forces, integrating European-influenced drill and tactics with the Sultanate's traditional cavalry and artillery traditions.

advances.name: Industrial Karkhanas
advances.text: The transformation of the Sultanate's royal workshops from court artisan operations into proto-industrial manufacturing centers, producing textiles, arms, and finished goods at scale.

advances.name: Legacy of Synthesis
advances.text: The enduring achievement of the Delhi Sultanate: the creation of a composite Indo-Islamic civilization that synthesized Persian, Turkish, Arabic, and Indian traditions into something greater than any single source.

destiny.name: Destiny of Delhi
destiny.text: The Sultanate of Delhi stands restored. Now begins the work of shaping its future, whether through the sword or through the pen. Achieve stability to unlock your chosen destiny path.

event.title: The Destiny of Delhi
event.text: The Sultanate has been restored, and with it the promise of a future worthy of Delhi's ancient grandeur. The Sultan must now chart the course that will carry this empire through the ages. The path is chosen, now it must be walked.

destiny.name: Deccan Conquest
destiny.text: The Deccan is slipping from Delhi's hand. Warangal has thrown out the Sultan's governor, and the Raichur country between the rivers is held by the new kingdom of Vijayanagar. Bring Warangal and Raichur under the Sultan's banner, as Alauddin Khalji once dreamed, and raise an army worthy of the enterprise.

conditions.text: Own Warangal, or a subject owns it
Own Raichur, or a subject owns it

event.title: The March into the Deccan
event.text: The Sultan's armies have crossed the Vindhya Range and brought the cities of the Deccan to heel. Warangal, the old seat of the Kakatiya kings, and Raichur between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra now fly Delhi's standard. The Deccan campaigns of Alauddin Khalji have been replicated, and this time, the gains shall be permanent. The wealth of the plateau flows north to Delhi, and the Hindu kingdoms of the south watch with growing alarm.

destiny.name: Subjugate the South
destiny.text: With the northern Deccan secured, the Sultan's gaze turns to the great Hindu kingdom of the south. Vijayanagar must fall. Build up Daulatabad, the second capital in the Deccan, so that the campaign can be sustained from it.

conditions.text: Own Vijayanagar, or a subject owns it
We own Daulatabad and its development is at least 35

event.title: The Southern Campaigns
event.text: Daulatabad has grown into a second capital, and from it the armies marched south. The mighty citadel of Vijayanagar, that last great bastion of Hindu resistance, has submitted to the Sultan's authority, and its treasure has been carted north. The southern campaigns have proven the Sultanate's military supremacy beyond any doubt. Now the Sultan must decide how to consolidate these vast new conquests.

options.text: March with war elephants at the vanguard.

modifiers.name: War Elephants of the Sultan
modifiers.text: The captured war elephants of the southern kingdoms now form the vanguard of the Sultan's armies, though their rampaging charges leave devastation in their wake.

modifiers.name: Scorched Earth Policy
modifiers.text: Ruthless suppression of resistance across the Deccan ensures compliance, though the methods employed tarnish the Sultan's reputation.

destiny.name: Sultan of All India
destiny.text: From the Himalayas to Cape Comorin, from the Indus to the Bay of Bengal: the Sultan's writ must run unchallenged. Take Madurai, Goa, and Thatta on the Indus. Command the mightiest army and the richest treasury in all the subcontinent.

conditions.text: Own Madurai, or a subject owns it
Own Goa, or a subject owns it
Own Thatta, or a subject owns it

event.title: Sultan of All India
event.text: From the snowy passes of Kashmir to the temple cities of the Tamil coast, from the wharves of Surat to the mangrove swamps of the Sundarbans: the Sultan's writ runs unchallenged across the entire subcontinent. No ruler since Ashoka has commanded such a domain. The question that now defines the empire is whether this universal sovereignty should be maintained through perpetual holy war, or whether the Sultan should seek a lasting peace among the peoples of India.

options.text: The ghazi sword must never rest.

modifiers.name: Ghazi Tradition
modifiers.text: The Sultan claims the title of ghazi, warrior of the faith, and perpetual expansion becomes the empire's raison d'etre, though constant warfare strains the treasury.

options.text: Let the peoples of India know peace.

modifiers.name: Pax Sultanica
modifiers.text: With all of India under one banner, the Sultan inaugurates an era of internal peace and religious accommodation, though the cessation of conquest breeds complacency among the ruling class and the armies are slow to rally.

destiny.name: Bengal Integration
destiny.text: Bengal, the wealthiest province in all of Hindustan, has been governed as a distant frontier for too long. Bring Gaur and Sonargaon under direct imperial administration, held by the Sultan himself and by no governor or subject prince, and harness the region's silk and rice wealth.

event.title: The Wealth of Bengal
event.text: The Sultan's administrators have completed the integration of Bengal into the imperial system. Gaur, that ancient capital of the Bengal sultans, and Sonargaon, the great emporium of the eastern delta, are now directly governed provinces of the Sultanate. Bengali silk, muslin, and rice flow west along the Grand Trunk Road, enriching the treasury and feeding the cities of Hindustan. The empire's economic center of gravity has shifted eastward.

destiny.name: Institutional Zenith
destiny.text: The Sultan's administration must extend its reach to the trading ports of western India. Bring Diu on the coast of Saurashtra into the imperial fold, fill the treasury, and build up Jaunpur on the Gomti into a city of scholars and officials.

conditions.text: Own Diu, or a subject owns it
We own Jaunpur and its development is at least 49

event.title: The Institutional Zenith
event.text: The Sultanate's administration has reached an unprecedented level of sophistication. With the ports of Gujarat under imperial control, revenue flows from every corner of the subcontinent to Delhi. The madrasas of Jaunpur produce a steady stream of trained administrators, and the sarkar system ensures that the Sultan's edicts are enforced from the Indus to the Brahmaputra. The question now is whether to pursue this administrative excellence through spiritual harmony or through systematic revenue extraction.

options.text: Embrace the Sufi path of tolerance.

modifiers.name: Sufi Tolerance
modifiers.text: The mystical traditions of Sufism bridge the divide between Muslim rulers and Hindu subjects, fostering commercial trust and diplomatic goodwill, though the emphasis on harmony makes the court reluctant to wage war.

modifiers.name: Imperial Revenue Survey
modifiers.text: A comprehensive survey of every field, workshop, and market stall in the empire provides the foundation for systematic taxation, strengthening provincial loyalty but diverting resources from intelligence gathering.

destiny.name: Beacon of Hindustan
destiny.text: The Sultanate must become the greatest administrative state the subcontinent has ever known. Secure the port of Chittagong, attain the highest prestige, and build Delhi itself to twice its size.

conditions.text: Own Chittagong, or a subject owns it
We own Delhi and its development is at least 82

event.title: Beacon of Hindustan
event.text: The Sultanate of Delhi has become what the Tughlaq emperors only dreamed of: a state whose administrative reach, cultural sophistication, and economic power are unmatched anywhere in the world. Scholars from Cairo to Samarkand journey to Delhi to study its systems of governance. The Sultan presides over a cosmopolitan court where Persian poetry and Sanskrit philosophy exist side by side, where Hindu temple mathematics informs Islamic astronomical tables, and where the diverse peoples of the subcontinent have found a shared identity under the banner of enlightened sovereignty.

options.text: Foster a cosmopolitan court for all peoples.

modifiers.name: Cosmopolitan Court
modifiers.text: Delhi's court becomes a beacon for scholars, diplomats, and poets from across the known world, expanding the Sultanate's diplomatic reach and influence.

options.text: Endow waqf foundations across the realm.

modifiers.name: Waqf Endowments
modifiers.text: Vast charitable endowments fund mosques, hospitals, and caravanserais across the empire. The scholars and imams who live on them are bound to the throne by its pious generosity.

units.name: Mamluk Guard Cavalry
units.text: Elite mounted warriors trained from youth in the Central Asian tradition, forming the Sultan's personal guard and the shock force of the Sultanate's armies.

units.name: Hasham Infantry
units.text: Conscripted foot soldiers drawn from the peasant population and paid in cash. Though less prestigious than the cavalry, their numbers gave the Sultanate its manpower advantage.

units.name: Barqandaz
units.text: Swift mounted archers specializing in harassing fire and rapid pursuit, employing Central Asian steppe tactics on the plains of Hindustan.

units.name: Topchi
units.text: Gunpowder artillerymen who crewed the Sultan's cannon batteries, drawn from a mix of Central Asian, Ottoman, and native traditions.

units.name: Suri Piyada
units.text: Disciplined infantrymen of the Suri era, drilled and equipped to a professional standard, representing a shift from feudal levy to standing army.

buildings.name: Tughlaqabad Fortress
buildings.text: A massive fortification built in the austere Tughlaq style, with sloping rubble-masonry walls and battered ramparts designed to withstand siege warfare.

buildings.name: Sarai
buildings.text: A walled roadside rest house providing food, shelter, and fresh horses for travelers and merchants along the trunk routes of the empire.

buildings.name: Firuz Shahi Madrasa
buildings.text: A royal college on the model of the one at Hauz Khas. Law, tradition and the sciences are taught by salaried masters, and the judges and secretaries of the sultan's service are drawn from its students.

buildings.name: Royal Karkhana
buildings.text: A state-owned workshop where master craftsmen produce arms, fine textiles, and luxury goods for the Sultan's court and armies.

buildings.name: Diwan-i-Arz
buildings.text: The military secretariat responsible for maintaining muster rolls, branding cavalry horses, and ensuring the readiness and discipline of the Sultan's armed forces.

buildings.name: Dar al-Shuja'a
buildings.text: The House of the Brave: an elite military academy where the Sultan's finest warriors are trained in horsemanship, siege craft, and the art of commanding armies across the vast distances of the subcontinent.

buildings.name: Firuzabad Complex
buildings.text: A grand administrative and cultural complex modeled on the vision of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, housing libraries, observatories, and the offices of the imperial bureaucracy.

list.name: Diwan-i-Wizarat
list.text: The wazir's office, central organ of the sultanate's revenue administration. The diwan drew up the kharaj rolls, audited the provincial bureaus, and transmitted the sultan's fiscal commands across Hindustan. Khwaja Khatir served Iltutmish in this office; Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul guided the late decades of Firuz Shah Tughluq from it. A capable wazir could keep the treasury filled even through dynastic crisis, but the office's vast discretion made the wazir himself the second man in the realm and an inevitable rival of the throne's other servitors.

list.name: Dabir-i-Khas
list.text: The sultan's confidential secretary and his office of clerks. They wrote the firmans, the diplomas of appointment and the sultan's letters in the high Persian of the court, in a land where almost no one spoke it at home. Amir Khusrau, the court's poet, wrote a manual of letter writing in that style in 1319. A firman read out in a newly taken town told its people whose they were, and a trained office let Delhi speak to provinces months away. When it decayed under the later Tughluqs, the provinces stopped listening.

list.name: Diwan-i-Risalat
list.text: The bureau of religious affairs and outgoing correspondence to foreign Muslim courts, charged with appointing qadis, recommending muftis, and drafting embassies. The diwan gave the ulama a recognized institutional channel to the throne and made the sultanate's diplomacy with the Abbasid Caliph in Mamluk Cairo, with the Ilkhanid and later Timurid courts, and with the rulers of Yemen and Mecca a matter of formal record. Empowered ulama insulated the sultan against accusations of impiety; left unchecked, the same ulama could declare a sultan an apostate.

list.name: Shahna-i-Mandi
list.text: The market superintendent established by Alauddin Khalji circa 1296-1316, who fixed the price of grain, cloth, slaves, and cattle in the Delhi mandis and forbade hoarding under penalty of physical mutilation. The reform fed a vast standing army by collapsing soldier wages while keeping rural producers' purchase prices low, but it depended on aggressive enforcement, ruined the merchants of the capital, and was abandoned within months of Alauddin's death. Barani recorded the policy as an unrepeatable masterpiece of statecraft, and as a warning.

list.name: Sadr-us-Sudur
list.text: The chief overseer of charitable endowments (waqf), appointer of imams to congregational mosques, and distributor of state stipends to scholars (idrar). Firuz Shah Tughluq endowed waqfs on a monumental scale: the karkhanas of Firuzabad, the great Hisar canal, and the founding of Jaunpur and Hisar-Firuza all flowed through this office. The Sadr maintained the registers of pious foundations and disbursed their income; in the right hands the office made the sultan a builder of mosques and madrasas remembered for centuries.

list.name: Naib-i-Mulk
list.text: The regent-vizierate, an extraordinary office in which a great noble assumed the powers of the sultan during minorities, ill health, or political incapacity. Khusrau Khan deposed Mubarak Khalji from this office in 1320; Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul ran Firuz Shah's later decades from it; Bahlul Lodi rose from a kind of vice-regency in the 1450s to found the last sultanate dynasty. The institution kept the realm functioning through weak sultans, but it concentrated the realm's military and fiscal levers in the hands of one noble, and produced more than one dynastic transition along the way.

list.name: Doab Cadaster
list.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq's project of 1325-1351 to measure every parcel in the Doab between the Ganges and Yamuna and to standardize revenue assessment by the cubit, supplanting older estimate-by-village methods. Combined with simultaneous tax hikes during drought, the cadaster precipitated peasant flight and a famine that depopulated whole districts. The administrative apparatus survived the catastrophe and became the model for the land surveys of Sher Shah Suri and, two centuries later, Akbar's Todar Mal: the foundations of Mughal fiscal sophistication were laid here.
